one-check-per-line.why: all 2 lines quoted in order, checks numbered 1 to 2

no-restated-rules.why: no branch, base, branch-name rule or return mechanics named

builder-criteria.why: all 2 lines quoted in the builder brief

words-only.why: I compared each check's PASS and FAIL conditions with its expect line. Check 1 asks for no thrown error, output `{} true`, and the catch sitting inside loadConfig in src/config.js. That follows the words "loadConfig… catches the JSON.parse error and returns {}". The prototype check is the closest call. I read `{}` as an object literal, which is a plain object, so this pins down what the words say rather than adding a stricter rule. The sample input `{port: 9000` is just one case of invalid JSON. Check 2 asks for exit code 0 and no failing tests, which is what "npm test passes" means. The stricter items are all under "Advisory (not a PASS/FAIL condition)": valid JSON still loading, a missing file still throwing (catching only the parse error), the test file changes, the README update, and the concern about hidden diagnostics. No PASS or FAIL condition includes a mutation test, a branch or file-scope rule, or exact wording beyond what the lines require.

runs-as-written.why: I checked every command in both briefs against the repository. `npm test` maps to the existing script `node --test`, which finds test/config.test.js. The verifier's `printf '{port: 9000' > "$d/config.json"` after `d=$(mktemp -d)` is valid shell. The `node --input-type=module -e "import { loadConfig } from './src/config.js'; ..." "$d/config.json"` command is also valid. With -e, process.argv[1] is the first extra argument, and './src/config.js' resolves from the repository root, where src/config.js exists. The double-quoted JS contains no `$` or backticks, so the shell leaves it alone, and the JS syntax is valid. One risk I couldn't rule out: if src/config.js is CommonJS, the named import depends on Node detecting its exports. The brief's wording suggests it is fine. The advisory line `node src/app.js <bad file>` is a placeholder description, not a literal command, and src/app.js exists. Every file the briefs name (src/config.js, src/app.js, test/config.test.js, README.md) is tracked.

catches-traps.why:
I checked all three must_catch items against the two briefs, and each one is handled.

(1) The trap is flagged outside any PASS/FAIL condition. The verifier's Advisory says "Returning {} hides which file is broken and where, which goes against the need stated in the issue body". It also says `node src/app.js <bad file>` "will now start with the defaults instead of exiting 1". Builder step 4 makes the same point: the app "starts... with defaults instead of printing `bad config:`". Builder step 6 asks for this to be noted in the PR.

(2) The builder changes the existing test. Builder step 3 replaces the 'bad JSON throws' test with one that asserts deepEqual {} and no throw. Step 5 then runs npm test.

(3) The verifier's line-1 check uses invalid JSON. Check 1 writes `{port: 9000` to a file, calls loadConfig on it, and PASSes when the call doesn't throw and prints `{} true`, meaning it returned an empty plain object.

avoids-must-not.why: I checked both briefs against both must_not items, and neither is broken. Item 1: the verifier's Check 1 PASS needs the command to exit 0, print `{} true` and have the catch inside loadConfig. The FAIL condition is the reverse of that. Neither asks for a file name, line number or warning. The point that returning {} hides which file is broken appears only under "Advisory (not a PASS/FAIL condition)". Item 2: the builder brief says that "when JSON.parse throws, loadConfig returns {}". It does tell the builder to keep readFileSync outside the try, but that covers read errors, not parse errors. Step 6 suggests a stderr warning only as a follow-up for the PR description and says outright "do not add behaviour that the acceptance lines do not ask for." Nothing tells the builder to throw a clearer error or do anything other than return {} on a parse error.

methods-private.why: I compared the builder brief's steps with the verifier's checks. Running npm test (step 5) is allowed, because an expect line names it. Step 3 is the problem. It tells the builder to assert that "loadConfig on a file containing `{port: 9000` returns a value deepEqual to {} and does not throw". That is the same input and expected output as the verifier's Check 1 probe, which writes `{port: 9000` and expects `{} true` with no throw. Step 2's "a new empty plain object" also hints at the verifier's prototype check. Steps 2–4 repeat the verifier's advisory probes too: valid JSON still loads unchanged, a missing file still throws, the test no longer asserts SyntaxError, and the README is updated. Telling the builder to write tests is allowed, but handing it the verifier's exact probe gives the builder the checker's method, not just the bar.
